```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")

OUT  <- "model_output"; SUPP <- file.path(OUT, "supp"); ISO <- file.path(OUT, "isochrones")
num  <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
rd   <- function(f) tryCatch(read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)

# --- reproducible sample numbers from the enriched call log ------------------
d <- read.csv(file.path("data/processed/ent_phase2_enriched.csv"), colClasses = "character")
comp <- d[d$complete == "Complete" & d$ent_type != "", ]
comp$offered <- comp$appointment_offered == "TRUE"
comp$w <- num(comp$wait_days_business)
N_total <- nrow(d); N_complete <- sum(d$complete == "Complete"); N_analytic <- nrow(comp)
N_off <- sum(comp$offered); pct_off <- 100 * mean(comp$offered)
N_samp <- sum(comp$appointment_outcome == "With sampled physician", na.rm = TRUE)
pct_samp <- 100 * N_samp / N_analytic
# offer-category counts restricted to actual offers, so they sum to N_off
N_diff    <- sum(comp$offered & comp$appointment_outcome == "With different physician", na.rm = TRUE)
N_app     <- sum(comp$offered & comp$appointment_outcome == "With APP only", na.rm = TRUE)
N_uncoded <- N_off - N_samp - N_diff - N_app
N_wait <- sum(!is.na(comp$w)); med_wait <- median(comp$w[comp$offered], na.rm = TRUE)
# cumulative probability of securing an appointment by day d, with no-offer calls
# retained as never obtaining one (denominator = all analytic calls)
cum_appt <- function(d) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * sum(comp$offered & !is.na(comp$w) & comp$w <= d) / N_analytic)
q_wait <- quantile(comp$w[comp$offered], c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)

# --- effect extractor: pull OR/IRR (95% CI, p) for a term from a model CSV ---
eff <- function(csv, term, col) {
  x <- rd(csv); if (is.null(x)) return("[NA]")
  r <- x[x$term == term, ]; if (!nrow(r)) return("[NA]")
  p <- num(r$p_value)
  sprintf("%.2f (95%% CI %.2f–%.2f; p%s)", num(r[[col]]), num(r$ci_lower), num(r$ci_upper),
          if (p < 0.001) " < 0.001" else sprintf(" = %.3f", p))
}
acc <- function(term) eff(file.path(OUT, "part1_access_OR.csv"), term, "or")
irr <- function(term) eff(file.path(OUT, "part2_wait_IRR.csv"), term, "irr")

# --- reviewer-response analyses: global tests, dual outcomes, callers, clustering ---
gtest <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S14_global_subspecialty_test.csv"))
gp <- function(part) {                        # joint LRT of the whole ent_type factor
  if (is.null(gtest)) return("[NA]")
  r <- gtest[grepl(part, gtest[["Model part"]]), ]; if (!nrow(r)) return("[NA]")
  sprintf("χ² = %.1f, df = %d, p = %.2f", num(r[["Chi-square"]]), num(r$df), num(r[["p-value"]]))
}
callr <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S12_caller_effects.csv"))
caller_p <- if (is.null(callr)) NULL else num(callr[["p-value"]])
caller_or_range <- if (is.null(callr)) "[NA]" else {
  v <- num(sub(" .*", "", callr[["Access OR (95% CI)"]][caller_p < 0.05])); sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(v), max(v))
}
caller_n_sig <- if (is.null(callr)) NA else sum(caller_p < 0.05 & callr$Caller != "Other")
dualo <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S13_dual_access_outcomes.csv"))
dsamp <- function(sub) {                      # stricter sampled-physician access OR
  if (is.null(dualo)) return("[NA]")
  r <- dualo[dualo[[1]] == sub, ]; if (!nrow(r)) return("[NA]")
  sprintf("OR %s; p = %.2f", r[["Sampled physician: OR (95% CI)"]], num(r[["Sampled physician: p"]]))
}
clus  <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S11_clustering_sensitivity.csv"))
fjt   <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S14b_factor_joint_tests.csv"))
jt <- function(factor_re, part_re) {                 # joint LRT string from S14b
  if (is.null(fjt)) return("[NA]")
  r <- fjt[grepl(factor_re, fjt$Factor) & grepl(part_re, fjt[["Model part"]]), ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return("[NA]")
  sprintf("χ² = %.1f, df = %d, p = %s", num(r[["Chi-square"]][1]), num(r$df[1]),
          if (num(r[["p-value"]][1]) < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("%.3f", num(r[["p-value"]][1])))
}
caller_gp     <- jt("Caller", "Access")              # caller, access (offer)
caller_gp_wt  <- jt("Caller", "Timeliness")          # caller, timeliness (wait)
jt_p <- function(factor_re, part_re) {               # compact p-value only
  if (is.null(fjt)) return("[NA]")
  r <- fjt[grepl(factor_re, fjt$Factor) & grepl(part_re, fjt[["Model part"]]), ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return("[NA]")
  p <- num(r[["p-value"]][1]); if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("%.3f", p)
}
gp_p <- function(part) { if (is.null(gtest)) return("[NA]")
  r <- gtest[grepl(part, gtest[["Model part"]]), ]; sprintf("%.2f", num(r[["p-value"]][1])) }
baltests <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S12c_balance_tests.csv"))
balp <- function(re) if (is.null(baltests)) "[NA]" else
  sprintf("p = %.2f", num(baltests[["p-value"]][grepl(re, baltests$Comparison)]))
dw    <- rd(file.path(SUPP, "S15_design_weighted.csv"))
wt_off_str <- if (is.null(dw)) "[NA]" else dw[["Design-weighted to frame (rural 7%)"]][grepl("offer", dw$Estimate)]

body_wc <- if (is.null(wc)) "≈ 4,200" else sprintf("%s words", format(wc$body[1], big.mark = ","))
```

## Abstract

**Objective.** To characterize subspecialty- and geography-related differences in access to and timeliness of otolaryngology (ENT) care in the United States using a national simulated-patient design.

**Methods.** In a cross-sectional mystery-caller study, trained callers requested new-patient appointments from a national, rurality-balanced sample of board-certified otolaryngologists using subspecialty-matched scripts. Two outcomes were modeled with a two-part (hurdle) approach, whether any appointment was *offered* and the *business-day wait* among offers, adjusting for subspecialty, geographic and payer context, and rurality, with a market-level random intercept. Subspecialty and caller were tested jointly, not by reference-category contrasts alone.

**Results.** Of `r N_total` calls, `r N_analytic` complete calls with a known subspecialty were analyzed. An appointment was offered in `r N_off` (`r sprintf('%.1f', pct_off)`%), but only `r N_samp` (`r sprintf('%.1f', pct_samp)`%) were with the physician requested; the median wait was `r med_wait` business days (IQR `r q_wait[1]`–`r q_wait[2]`). Subspecialty was **not** jointly associated with either outcome (offer p = `r gp_p('Access')`, wait p = `r gp_p('Timeliness')`). In the primary any-offer model the only nominally significant subspecialty contrast was pediatric otolaryngology (OR `r acc('ent_typePediatrics')`), which did not carry to the with-the-requested-physician outcome or survive multiplicity adjustment. No geographic covariate was associated with either outcome. Appointment offers instead varied clearly by trained caller (joint p = `r jt_p('Caller','Access')`), clearer statistical evidence of association than subspecialty; conditional wait time was associated with none of caller (p = `r jt_p('Caller','Timeliness')`), subspecialty, or geography.

**Conclusions.** The clearest finding was attrition: only about half of calls to board-certified otolaryngologists yielded an appointment with the physician sought. Whether an appointment was offered varied more clearly by caller than by measured subspecialty or geography, while wait times were not conclusively associated with either. Availability and timeliness are distinct dimensions of access and should be measured separately.

**Keywords:** otolaryngology; access to care; health services accessibility; simulated patient; mystery caller; appointment wait time; rural health; workforce.

**Running head:** Subspecialty and geography in otolaryngology access.

## Introduction

Otolaryngologic conditions, from chronic rhinosinusitis and otitis media to airway disorders and head-and-neck malignancy, are among the most common reasons patients seek specialty care, and for many of these conditions timely evaluation influences diagnosis and outcome, with delays in the diagnosis-to-treatment interval associated with worse survival in head-and-neck cancer [@graboyes2019]. Whether a new patient can actually reach an otolaryngologist, however, is not guaranteed by the presence of physicians in a region; it depends on whether an office will offer an appointment and, if so, how long the patient must wait.

Access to specialty care thus has two distinct dimensions that are often conflated: *availability*, whether a new-patient appointment is offered at all, and *timeliness*, how quickly the patient is seen. These dimensions can move independently: an office that readily books new patients may nonetheless carry a long queue, and measuring only one can mislead. Administrative and survey data capture both imperfectly, reflecting patients who have already navigated the system and remaining subject to recall and reporting bias.

Simulated-patient ("mystery caller") studies address this gap by having trained callers pose as new patients and request appointments under a standardized script, directly measuring the experience a real patient would encounter [@bisgaier2011]. The design has been applied across specialties to reveal access barriers invisible in claims data. Within otolaryngology, the correlates of new-patient access remain incompletely characterized. Two classes of factor are plausible: the *clinical* nature of the request, the requested subspecialty (general otolaryngology versus pediatric otolaryngology, laryngology, head-and-neck oncology, and others), and the *contextual* environment of the practice, local physician supply, the state Medicaid fee level, community social vulnerability, the share of dual-eligible beneficiaries, and rurality [@vickery2016]. Because each subspecialty was approached with its own clinically appropriate vignette, the requested subspecialty and the clinical scenario are inseparable in this design; we therefore treat subspecialty as a combined "who is asked, for what" exposure rather than a property of the physician alone.

We conducted a national mystery-caller study of board-certified otolaryngologists to characterize how the requested subspecialty and the geographic-contextual environment relate to (1) whether a new-patient appointment is offered and (2) the business-day wait when one is offered. To keep these two dimensions of access distinct, we analyzed them with a two-part model.

## Methods

### Study design and sample

We conducted a cross-sectional, simulated-patient ("mystery caller") study of access to otolaryngology (ENT) care in the United States [@rankin2022]. Trained callers telephoned a national sample of practicing, board-certified otolaryngologists and, following a standardized script, requested a new-patient appointment for a subspecialty-matched chief complaint. Each sampled physician was contacted once. The sampling frame was the American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery roster of board-certified otolaryngologists practicing in the United States (N = 11,333), linked to National Provider Identifier records for practice location and rurality. Because rural otolaryngologists were scarce in this frame (791 of 11,333; 7.0%), we drew a rurality-stratified sample of 480 urban and 480 rural physicians (960 total) to obtain balanced representation; the rural stratum accordingly included a majority of all rural board-certified otolaryngologists in the frame. Calls were placed between May 29 and July 6, 2026, to physicians in 48 states, each under a commercial Blue Cross Blue Shield insurance scenario held constant across calls, with the chief complaint matched to the sampled physician's subspecialty (general otolaryngology, facial plastic surgery, head and neck oncology, laryngology, otology/neurotology, pediatric otolaryngology, rhinology, or sleep medicine). Script selection followed the physician's fellowship training (subspecialty-specific script if fellowship-trained, otherwise the general otolaryngology script), and callers verified board certification and coded practice rurality before each call; the full pre-call procedure and the verbatim subspecialty scripts are provided in the Supplementary Appendix (**Table S9**). *[To confirm from the protocol: the number and timing of call attempts before a physician was recorded as unreachable, and caller-training procedures.]* The Human Subjects Protection Program at Old Dominion University (Macon &amp; Joan Brock Virginia Health Sciences / Eastern Virginia Medical School) determined that this project (IRB #24-12-NH-0285) does not involve human subjects research and is therefore not subject to IRB review; informed consent was not required. The covert measurement of clinician behavior has been debated, most publicly when a 2011 federally commissioned "mystery shopper" survey of primary-care access was shelved amid concern about deceiving physician practices [@rhodes2011; @blinkhorn2013], but a formal ethical analysis has since established that simulated-patient research without prior consent is justified when risks and burdens are minimal, a consent waiver is necessary for scientifically valid data, and the study carries substantial social value [@rhodesmiller2012]. This study was designed to satisfy those conditions. Consistent with established simulated-patient practice, the covert design incorporated several safeguards: no protected health information was collected and no calls were recorded; each contact was a single brief call that booked no real appointment and imposed minimal burden on office staff; and identifying information about individual staff members was neither requested nor stored. Covert simulated calling was necessary because non-covert methods, for example, surveys of offices aware of being observed, would systematically bias access estimates through social desirability, the same rationale that underlies the design's measurement validity [@moriarty2003; @hodson2025; @rankin2022]. Aggregate, market-level findings will be made available through specialty-society and state channels as a benefit to participating communities, in the spirit of the participant-feedback provisions used in prior covert simulated-patient studies [@lungfiel2023].

Analyses were restricted to calls with a completed data-collection record and a determinable physician subspecialty. This study did not manipulate patient insurance; the exposures of interest were the requested subspecialty and the geographic context of the practice.

### Outcomes

Two outcomes were analyzed as a two-part (hurdle) process. The primary *access* outcome was whether the office offered any new-patient appointment (binary), counting an appointment with the sampled physician, with another physician in the same practice, or with an advanced practice provider; a call was coded as no offer when no appointment date was offered, including cases in which the sampled physician had retired, left, or was not accepting new patients and no alternative appointment date was offered. Because "getting in the door" and "seeing the specific specialist sought" are not the same, we also analyzed a stricter secondary outcome, an appointment specifically with the sampled physician, and report both (**Table S13**). The *timeliness* outcome was the number of **business days** from the call to the next available appointment, counted excluding weekends and U.S. federal holidays, and defined only for calls in which an appointment was offered. We recorded the *first*-available appointment; prior simulated-patient work has shown that the more elaborate third-next-available metric adds little beyond first-available while reducing reliability [@campbell2013]. Of the appointment offers, a small number lacked a recorded next-available date; these contribute to the access analysis but not the timeliness analysis, which is noted where the analytic denominators are reported.

### Geographic covariates

Each practice was linked to contextual covariates by practice ZIP code and state. County was assigned from a 2020 Census ZCTA-to-county crosswalk (dominant county by land area). Covariates comprised: county otolaryngologist supply per 100,000 population; the state Medicaid-to-Medicare fee index (Kaiser Family Foundation, 2024, all services) [@kfffee]; the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI, 2022, tract-level, population-weighted to the practice ZIP) [@cdcsvi]; the county fraction of Medicare beneficiaries dual-eligible for Medicaid (CMS); metropolitan hospital-market concentration (Herfindahl–Hirschman Index [HHI], KFF 2024; available for metropolitan areas only); rurality, dichotomized from Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes as urban (RUCA 1–3) versus rural (RUCA 4–10); and the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS) Board of Governors region.

### Statistical analysis

Because wait time is defined only after an appointment offer, we modeled the two components separately: appointment *offer* among all analytic calls (mixed-effects logistic regression) and *conditional wait time* among calls receiving an offer (mixed-effects negative binomial regression). The timeliness component is therefore explicitly conditional on an offer, and its estimates describe waits among those offered rather than the unselected population. The negative binomial distribution was selected over Poisson on the basis of substantial overdispersion (Pearson φ = 6.22). Both models included a random intercept for core-based statistical area (CBSA; county FIPS where CBSA was undefined) to account for within-market correlation, and adjusted for the requested subspecialty (reference: general otolaryngology), county ENT supply, Medicaid fee index, SVI, dual-eligible fraction, and rurality (reference: urban). The identity of the caller (research assistant) was included as a fixed effect. Continuous covariates were standardized and, for the few missing values (<3%), median-imputed.

Because subspecialty and caller are multi-level factors, each was assessed with a joint (multi–degree-of-freedom) likelihood-ratio test of the whole factor, reported before any reference-category contrast; pairwise subspecialty differences were adjusted for multiplicity by the Tukey method. Reference-category odds ratios and rate ratios are reported for completeness but interpreted only in light of the joint tests. To avoid conflating "getting any appointment" with "seeing the specialist sought," access was modeled for both the primary any-offer outcome and the stricter with-the-sampled-physician outcome (**Table S13**). Because the caller factor proved jointly significant rather than a mere nuisance, caller odds ratios are reported in full (**Table S12**), the balance of callers across subspecialty, rurality, and region is tabulated (**Table S12c**), and the headline subspecialty estimate was re-examined in a leave-one-caller-out analysis (**Table S12b**). Although each physician was sampled once, some calls reached a shared practice telephone number (670 distinct numbers among the analytic calls); for **both** outcomes we confirmed that adding a practice–telephone random intercept and refitting on one call per number left the estimates essentially unchanged (**Table S11**). Because the rurality-balanced design over-samples rural practices, offer rates and waits are reported both unweighted (describing the analytic sample) and design-weighted to the frame's rural prevalence (**Table S15**). As bounding sensitivity analyses for the excluded incomplete calls, we recomputed the offer rate treating all incomplete calls first as offers and then as non-offers.

Effects are reported as odds ratios (access) and incidence rate ratios (timeliness) with 95% Wald confidence intervals. Pairwise differences between subspecialties were estimated with Tukey-adjusted estimated marginal means [@emmeans]. Effect modification of the geographic covariates by subspecialty was tested by likelihood-ratio tests. Market-level clustering was summarized by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Because the HHI is defined only in metropolitan areas, its association with timeliness was assessed in a sensitivity model restricted to the metropolitan subset. Two additional sensitivity analyses were performed: a three-level rurality specification (urban, RUCA 1–3; suburban, 4–6; rural, 7–10) in place of the binary contrast, and a complete-case refit that excluded records with any missing covariate rather than median-imputing them. Whether call incompleteness was related to the measured covariates was assessed with chi-square and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Analyses used R 4.4.2 [@rcoreteam] (packages `glmmTMB` [@glmmTMB], `emmeans` [@emmeans], and the study package `mysterycall`); two-sided α = 0.05. Reporting follows the STROBE guideline for observational studies [@strobe] and the simulated-patient–specific CRiSP/CRiSPHe reporting checklist [@crisp2021; @crisphe2024].

### Sample size and power

The power analysis was pre-specified before data collection, implemented in a purpose-built simulation application, and targeted 800 completed calls with the rural-versus-urban difference in business-day wait time as the primary contrast; to allow for incomplete calls, we sampled 960 physicians (480 urban and 480 rural), anticipating roughly 20% attrition to leave approximately 800 analyzable calls. Its assumptions were anchored to empirical data rather than convention: the expected rural wait penalty, the negative binomial dispersion (φ = 1.7), and the state-level intraclass correlation (ICC = 0.08) were estimated by pooling 273 rural otolaryngology observations from two published access series [@corbisiero2024; @saeedi2025]. Under these assumptions and a two-sided α = 0.05, 800 completed calls provided greater than 99% power to detect the anticipated eight-business-day rural–urban gap; the minimum detectable difference at 90% power was approximately six business days. The design was robust to two realistic threats: after a 20% non-response buffer (analyzable n ≈ 640) power remained near 98%, and although a balanced 50/50 rural/urban allocation was optimal, an unbalanced allocation at the ~15% rural prevalence reported in those source datasets still yielded 83% power. Rural otolaryngologists were in fact even scarcer in the present frame (791 of 11,333; 7.0%), so an unbalanced natural-prevalence sample would have produced very few rural calls; we therefore over-sampled rural physicians to the balanced 50/50 design. The realized dispersion (φ = 6.22) substantially exceeded the planned value, reducing achieved power relative to plan; the resulting reconciliation is reported in the *Limitations*.

## Results

### Sample and attrition

Callers placed `r N_total` calls; `r N_complete` (`r sprintf('%.1f', 100*N_complete/N_total)`%) were completed, of which `r N_analytic` had a determinable subspecialty and formed the analytic sample. Any new-patient appointment was offered in `r N_off` of `r N_analytic` (`r sprintf('%.1f', pct_off)`%; `r wt_off_str` when design-weighted to the frame's rural prevalence), but only `r N_samp` (`r sprintf('%.1f', pct_samp)`%) were with the specific physician requested; the median next-available wait among offers was `r med_wait` business days (IQR `r q_wait[1]`–`r q_wait[2]`). Of the `r N_total` physicians sampled, `r N_analytic` yielded a complete call with a determinable subspecialty; a further `r N_complete - N_analytic` calls were completed but the subspecialty could not be determined (all `r N_complete - N_analytic` were no-offer), and `r N_total - N_complete` calls were incomplete. Because incompleteness may itself represent an access barrier, we bounded its effect on the overall offer rate across all `r N_total` sampled physicians: `r sprintf('%.0f', 100*N_off/N_total)`% if none of the `r N_total - N_complete` incomplete calls would have produced an offer and `r sprintf('%.0f', 100*(N_off + (N_total - N_complete))/N_total)`% if all would have. Sample characteristics are shown in **Table 1**, and the participant flow in **Figure 1**.

```{r table1}
lv <- c("General", setdiff(names(sort(table(comp$ent_type), decreasing = TRUE)), "General"))
tb1 <- tibble::tibble(
  Subspecialty = factor(comp$ent_type, levels = lv),
  offered = factor(ifelse(comp$offered, "Offered", "Not offered"), levels = c("Offered", "Not offered")),
  wait = ifelse(comp$offered, comp$w, NA_real_),
  Rurality = factor(comp$ruca_category, levels = c("Urban", "Rural")),
  ent_per_100k = num(comp$ent_per_100k),
  medicaid_fee_index = num(comp$medicaid_fee_index),
  svi_overall = num(comp$svi_overall),
  dual_pct = num(comp$dual_pct))
gtsummary::tbl_summary(
    tb1, by = Subspecialty,
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})",
                     all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"),
    digits = list(ent_per_100k ~ 1, medicaid_fee_index ~ 2, svi_overall ~ 2, dual_pct ~ 2),
    label = list(offered ~ "Appointment offered", wait ~ "Business-day wait, if offered",
                 Rurality ~ "Rurality", ent_per_100k ~ "ENT per 100,000",
                 medicaid_fee_index ~ "Medicaid fee index", svi_overall ~ "Social Vulnerability Index",
                 dual_pct ~ "Dual-eligible fraction"),
    missing = "no") |>
  gtsummary::add_overall(last = FALSE) |>
  gtsummary::modify_header(label ~ "**Characteristic**") |>
  gtsummary::modify_spanning_header(gtsummary::all_stat_cols() ~ "**Requested subspecialty**") |>
  gtsummary::modify_caption("**Table 1. Sample characteristics by requested subspecialty.**") |>
  gtsummary::as_flex_table() |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all") |>
  flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1)
```

### Access to appointments

Requested subspecialty was **not** jointly associated with whether an appointment was offered (joint likelihood-ratio test across all subspecialties, `r gp('Access')`). Among the individual reference-category contrasts, only pediatric otolaryngology differed nominally from general otolaryngology, with roughly twice the odds of an offer (OR `r acc('ent_typePediatrics')`); otology/neurotology trended lower (OR `r acc('ent_typeOtology/neurotology')`). This single contrast was not robust. It did not carry to the stricter with-the-requested-physician outcome (`r dsamp('Pediatric otolaryngology')`), under which a different subspecialty (rhinology) was instead nominally significant (**Table S13**), an inconsistency in *which* subspecialty stands out that argues against a genuine subspecialty gradient. Across leave-one-caller-out refits the pediatric estimate stayed similar in magnitude (OR 2.1–2.7) but varied in nominal significance and in the joint subspecialty test (**Table S12b**), and no subspecialty pair reached significance after Tukey adjustment (Robustness and missing data). No geographic covariate was associated with access: county ENT supply (OR `r acc('ent_per_100k_z')` per SD), the Medicaid fee index (OR `r acc('medicaid_fee_index_z')`), social vulnerability (OR `r acc('svi_overall_z')`), and dual-eligibility (OR `r acc('dual_pct_z')`) were all null (**Figure 2**).

By contrast, whether an appointment was offered was **jointly associated with the trained caller** (`r caller_gp`; **Table S12**), which showed clearer statistical evidence of association than the subspecialty factor. `r caller_n_sig` callers had roughly two-fold higher adjusted odds of an offer than the reference caller (OR `r caller_or_range`). This is unlikely to be a confounded exposure: the callers' caseloads were balanced across subspecialty and rurality (Monte Carlo χ² tests, caller × subspecialty `r balp('subspecialty')`, caller × rurality `r balp('rurality')`; full distribution in **Table S12c**). The pattern is most consistent with encounter-level implementation, how the identical script was delivered and how ambiguous responses were recorded, although unmeasured differences in call timing cannot be fully excluded, and it bounds how finely a single simulated call can resolve true differences between practices. The caller association was specific to obtaining an offer; conditional wait time was not associated with caller (`r caller_gp_wt`).

### Timeliness of appointments

Among offering offices, subspecialty was not jointly associated with wait time (joint likelihood-ratio test, `r gp('Timeliness')`), though the overall test approached significance. In the reference-category contrasts, waits were longer for laryngology (IRR `r irr('ent_typeLaryngology')`) and pediatric otolaryngology (IRR `r irr('ent_typePediatrics')`) relative to general otolaryngology. These differences are also visible descriptively in the observed subspecialty medians (**Table S3**), which are the most reliable summary given the sparse counts in several subspecialties; we do not convert the rate ratios into calendar-week estimates, because an incidence-rate ratio scales a mean rather than the reported median. No geographic covariate was associated with wait time (**Figure 2**; **Table 2**). Combining both access dimensions, the cumulative probability that a call secured an appointment, counting calls with no offer as never obtaining one, was `r cum_appt(14)`% within 14 business days, `r cum_appt(30)`% within 30, and `r cum_appt(60)`% within 60 (**Figure S1**).

```{r table2}
a <- rd(file.path(OUT, "part1_access_OR.csv")); b <- rd(file.path(OUT, "part2_wait_IRR.csv"))
# human-readable labels for model coefficients
relabel <- function(term) {
  map <- c(
    "ent_typeFacial Plastics"      = "Facial plastic surgery",
    "ent_typeHead and Neck Cancer" = "Head and neck oncology",
    "ent_typeLaryngology"          = "Laryngology",
    "ent_typeOtology/neurotology"  = "Otology/neurotology",
    "ent_typePediatrics"           = "Pediatric otolaryngology",
    "ent_typeRhinology"            = "Rhinology",
    "ent_typeSleep"                = "Sleep medicine",
    "ent_per_100k_z"               = "Otolaryngologist density (per SD)",
    "medicaid_fee_index_z"         = "Medicaid fee index (per SD)",
    "svi_overall_z"                = "Social Vulnerability Index (per SD)",
    "dual_pct_z"                   = "Dual-eligible share (per SD)",
    "ruralRural"                   = "Rural (vs urban)",
    "ent_typeGeneral"              = "General otolaryngology (reference)",
    "(Intercept)"                  = "Intercept")
  out <- unname(map[term])
  cal <- grepl("^caller_f", term) & is.na(out)          # caller_fFalk -> "Caller: Falk"
  out[cal] <- paste0("Caller: ", sub("^caller_f", "", term[cal]))
  ifelse(is.na(out), term, out)
}
mk <- function(x, est) {
  if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
  x <- x[!grepl("caller|Intercept", x$term), ]
  data.frame(
    Term = relabel(x$term),
    Estimate = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", num(x[[est]]), num(x$ci_lower), num(x$ci_upper)),
    p = ifelse(num(x$p_value) < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", num(x$p_value))),
    check.names = FALSE)
}
ta <- mk(a, "or"); tb <- mk(b, "irr")
if (!is.null(ta)) { names(ta)[2] <- "OR (95% CI)"; ft(ta,
   "Table 2a. Access model (odds ratios). Subspecialty reference: general otolaryngology; rurality reference: urban.") }
```

```{r table2b}
if (!is.null(tb)) { names(tb)[2] <- "IRR (95% CI)"; ft(tb,
   "Table 2b. Timeliness model (incidence rate ratios). Subspecialty reference: general otolaryngology; rurality reference: urban.") }
```

### Secondary access measures

Beyond the two modeled outcomes, the call log captured several other steps of the access pathway (**Table S10**, **Figure S6**). Of the `r N_analytic` analytic calls, a live office was reached in `r sum(comp$office_answered=='TRUE',na.rm=TRUE)` (`r sprintf('%.0f', 100*mean(comp$office_answered=='TRUE',na.rm=TRUE))`%); the practice was accepting new patients in `r sum(comp$new_patient_status=='Accepting',na.rm=TRUE)` (`r sprintf('%.0f', 100*mean(comp$new_patient_status=='Accepting',na.rm=TRUE))`%); and an appointment was offered in `r N_off` (`r sprintf('%.0f', pct_off)`%). Critically, only `r N_samp` calls (`r sprintf('%.0f', pct_samp)`%) yielded an appointment **with the specific board-certified otolaryngologist requested**. The `r N_off` offers comprised `r N_samp` with the sampled physician, `r N_diff` (`r sprintf('%.0f', 100*N_diff/N_off)`%) with a different physician in the practice, `r N_app` with an advanced practice provider only, and `r N_uncoded` for which the provider category was not recorded (`r N_samp` + `r N_diff` + `r N_app` + `r N_uncoded` = `r N_off`); the four calls in which the sampled physician had retired, left, or was full and only a different physician was mentioned without an appointment being made were counted as no offer. Of the `r N_off` offers, `r N_off - N_wait` lacked an analyzable next-available date (`r N_off - N_wait - 1` never recorded and one with an erroneous appointment year, excluded) and so entered the access but not the timeliness analysis (`r N_wait` waits analyzed). These are overlapping measures of the same calls rather than a strictly nested funnel, a small number of offices offered an appointment without having affirmed on the call that they see the presented complaint, so the counts are not perfectly monotonic; **Figure S6** orders them by frequency for readability. Two front-desk barriers stood out: `r sum(comp$sees_chief_complaint=='No',na.rm=TRUE)` practices stated they do not see the presented complaint despite the sampled physician's matched subspecialty, and among practices not accepting new patients the most common documented reasons were that the physician had retired or left (`r sum(comp$new_patient_status=='Not accepting: retired/left',na.rm=TRUE)`) or an unspecified closure (`r sum(comp$new_patient_status=='Not accepting: unspecified',na.rm=TRUE)`), pointing to an apparent mismatch between roster listing and same-call schedulability at the contacted practice.

### Robustness and missing data

Consistent with the joint tests, no subspecialty pair reached significance under Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparison, and the subspecialty effect did not vary by rurality or supply (interaction likelihood-ratio tests, both non-significant). Market-level clustering was modest: the core-based statistical area random intercept accounted for a latent intraclass correlation of 0.043 in the access model (CBSA variance 0.26 on the log scale in the timeliness model), indicating that most variation in access and timeliness lay within rather than between markets. Because some calls reached a shared practice telephone number, we refit **both** the access and timeliness models with an added practice–telephone random intercept and, separately, on a single call per number; the practice-telephone variance was negligible and the estimates were essentially unchanged (**Table S11**), confirming that the CBSA-only model does not materially understate uncertainty from repeated practices. In a metropolitan sensitivity model, greater hospital-market concentration was associated with a borderline increase in wait time (HHI IRR 1.20 per SD; p = 0.058). Call incompleteness was unrelated to the measured practice geography; however, the recorded reasons for incompleteness were themselves missing for most incomplete calls, so we cannot fully characterize the missingness mechanism and treat the missing-at-random assumption as an approximation rather than an established fact (Supplement). The main findings were stable across two sensitivity analyses (**Table S8**). Under a three-level rurality specification (urban, RUCA 1–3; suburban, 4–6; rural, 7–10), no urban-to-rural gradient emerged, neither suburban (wait IRR 1.15) nor the sparse rural stratum (IRR 1.29) differed significantly from urban, while the subspecialty contrasts were unchanged. A complete-case analysis without imputation (n = 412 recorded waits) likewise reproduced the longer waits for laryngology (IRR 2.51) and pediatric otolaryngology (IRR 1.52) and the null rural–urban contrast (IRR 1.14).

## Discussion

In this national simulated-patient study of otolaryngology access, the most consistent finding was attrition along the access pathway: although a new-patient appointment was offered on roughly three-fifths of completed calls, only about half reached the specific board-certified otolaryngologist requested. Point estimates for individual subspecialty contrasts were sometimes sizeable but were imprecisely estimated and did not survive joint testing or multiplicity adjustment, and none of the measured contextual factors, county physician supply, Medicaid fee level, social vulnerability, dual-eligibility, or rurality, was associated with either outcome.

Three observations follow. First, **the gap between the listed and the reachable specialist is the most consistent signal.** Only half of calls to rostered, board-certified otolaryngologists yielded an appointment with the physician sought; among offers, nearly one in seven was with a different physician and additional offers were with an advanced practice provider only. Together with the frequency of "retired or left," "practice full," and "not accepting" responses, this identifies an apparent mismatch between roster listing and same-call schedulability at the contacted practice. We are careful not to equate this with directory error: a call may fail to reach the sampled physician because the physician is temporarily unavailable, requires a referral or records first, practices at another location, is not accepting new patients, or redirects the complaint to a partner, in addition to genuinely outdated listings, and front-desk statements were not independently verified. Even so, this same-call schedulability gap was documented more consistently than any subspecialty or geographic gradient, and independent validation of how much reflects outdated directory information versus current scheduling or referral policy is a clear next step.

Second, **availability and timeliness are distinct dimensions that can diverge.** Descriptively, pediatric otolaryngology was among the *easiest* subspecialties to reach yet carried one of the *longest* waits once an appointment was secured, and laryngology showed the longest waits of all. A patient-centered account of access must report both dimensions, because an intervention aimed at one will not necessarily improve the other. We emphasize, however, that these subspecialty differences were not statistically robust (below) and are best treated as hypothesis-generating.

Third, **the apparent subspecialty and geographic differences did not survive formal testing, and encounter-level implementation showed clearer evidence of association with obtaining an offer than either.** No subspecialty was jointly associated with access or timeliness; the single nominally significant contrast (pediatric otolaryngology for any offer) did not carry to the stricter with-the-requested-physician outcome (under which a different subspecialty was instead nominally significant) or to Tukey adjustment, and although its magnitude was stable across leave-one-caller-out refits its nominal significance and the joint subspecialty test were sensitive to which caller was excluded. By contrast, the caller factor was jointly significant for obtaining an offer (`r caller_gp`), clearer statistical evidence of association than the subspecialty factor, with individual callers differing roughly two-fold in the odds of an offer; the caller association was specific to the offer and absent for conditional wait time (`r caller_gp_wt`). We do not read the caller differences as effect magnitudes to be compared with the subspecialty coefficients, only as evidence that how a single call is conducted materially shapes the measured offer. Because each subspecialty was also tied to its own clinical vignette, any subspecialty difference additionally confounds the clinical scenario, and cannot be attributed to the physician's subspecialty alone. We therefore do not interpret subspecialty or geography as determinants of access. The null contextual findings argue against a simple supply-gradient model but are also compatible with the study being underpowered for modest gradients, particularly in the sparse rural stratum; absence of evidence here is not evidence of absence. Distinguishing this *contextual gradient* from the geographic *reach* of care, the travel burden a patient must overcome to arrive at a practice at all, is the subject of a companion geospatial analysis.

These findings point less toward a subspecialty- or region-specific intervention than toward the gap between being listed and being schedulable: the distinction between "a physician is listed" and "a new patient can actually be seen by that physician" deserves attention from directory maintainers, referral systems, and access researchers, once its causes are validated. That the measured contextual factors did not predict access does not exclude disparities not measured here, including patient insurance type, which this phase held constant.

**Strengths and limitations.** A central strength is the simulated-patient design itself: because offices were unaware of being observed, responses were insulated from the social-desirability and observation (Hawthorne) bias that affects surveys of practices aware they are being studied, yielding a more faithful measure of the experience a real new patient would encounter [@rankin2022]. The realized sample achieved the pre-specified, near-optimal urban/rural balance (approximately 50/50 under the RUCA 1–3 vs 4–10 dichotomy) and exceeded the planned call budget. Of the `r N_off` offers, `r N_off - N_wait` lacked an analyzable next-available date, `r N_off - N_wait - 1` never recorded and one with an implausible appointment year (a wait exceeding two years from a data-entry error), leaving `r N_wait` waits. The study was modestly underpowered for its primary rural-versus-urban timeliness contrast, and the realized negative-binomial dispersion (φ = 6.22) substantially exceeded the planned value, further reducing power; the observed rural–urban difference was small (about two business days) and non-significant, and its confidence interval (Table 2) conveys the remaining uncertainty. Each physician was contacted once, precluding within-physician inference; each call captured the response of a single office representative, whose account may not reflect the practice's full scheduling behavior; contextual covariates were linked at the ZIP-code or county level and thus approximate a practice's true environment; patient insurance was held constant (not varied) in this phase; and appointment availability reflects a single point in time. Several further limitations temper the subspecialty and geographic comparisons. Because each subspecialty was approached with its own clinically appropriate vignette (differing in patient age, urgency, and cancer risk), the requested subspecialty is confounded with the clinical scenario and cannot be isolated as a property of the physician; sleep-medicine physicians, moreover, were approached with the general script. Several subspecialty strata were sparse (for example, only 13 laryngology and 16 sleep physicians, with correspondingly few rural observations), limiting power for subspecialty-specific and subspecialty-by-rurality contrasts and making those estimates unstable. The caller factor was jointly significant for obtaining an offer, with clearer statistical evidence of association than subspecialty (**Table S12**, **S14b**); because callers were well balanced across subspecialty and rurality (**Table S12c**), this most likely reflects encounter-level implementation rather than a confounded exposure, though unmeasured differences in call timing cannot be excluded, and it cautions against over-interpreting modest between-practice differences from a single call. Drop-one likelihood-ratio statistics with differing degrees of freedom index the strength of statistical evidence, not comparative effect magnitude, and we interpret them accordingly. Although the sample spanned 48 states, it was drawn with a deliberate 50/50 rural/urban over-sample rather than in proportion to the workforce (which is ~93% urban); design-weighting to the frame's rural prevalence changed the offer rate only marginally (**Table S15**) because offer rates were similar across strata, but the reported figures nonetheless describe this stratified sample and should not be read as nationally representative population estimates. Finally, the study measured whether an appointment was offered and how long the wait was, but did not adjudicate the accuracy of front-desk statements, so the schedulability gap we describe is an observation from the call log rather than an independently verified measure of directory accuracy.

**Future directions.** Several extensions follow directly from this design. First, because insurance was held constant, a natural next phase is to vary the payer (e.g., Medicaid vs commercial) within the same frame; a prior specialty-cancer mystery-caller study that likewise fixed insurance identified this as its principal next step [@pollack2016]. Second, most otolaryngology care is physician-referred, so our patient-initiated calls capture a self-referral ceiling; a complementary arm in which the caller poses as a referring primary-care office would better reflect the true specialist-referral pathway [@pollack2016]. Third, our secondary measures hint at an information-quality dimension we did not fully model, whether front-desk statements (that a practice does not see a complaint, or that a physician is unavailable) are accurate, which simulated-patient studies increasingly treat as a distinct outcome, "available ≠ accessible ≠ accurately communicated" [@wilkinson2018]. Comparing publicly listed directory or website information against phone-obtained access would quantify this gap directly [@hodson2025], and the frequency of "retired or left" responses in our data suggests provider directories materially overstate the reachable workforce. Finally, whether schedulers appropriately triage clinically urgent presentations, head-and-neck cancer red flags, for instance, is an access-quality axis beyond the offer and wait we measured [@moriarty2003].

**Conclusion.** In a national mystery-caller study, only about half of calls to rostered board-certified otolaryngologists secured an appointment with the specific physician sought, while differences by subspecialty and by local supply, Medicaid fee level, or social vulnerability were imprecisely estimated and not robust to joint testing or multiplicity adjustment. Availability and timeliness were distinct dimensions of access, and both were shaped as much by how the request was handled as by where the patient lived. Future access studies should distinguish being listed from being schedulable, and should measure both whether patients can get in and how long they wait.

## Supplementary Appendix: Standardized call script

Callers followed a standardized telephone script, presenting as a new patient (or a family member calling on a patient's behalf) with a referral-based, subspecialty-matched chief complaint, and recorded responses in a structured data-capture form.

**Pre-call procedure.** Before each call, the caller searched the sampled physician's name and state of practice online and identified the matching practice website (typically among the first results, in under one minute). From the website, the caller determined whether the physician was fellowship-trained and selected the correspondingly matched subspecialty script; if the physician was not fellowship-trained, or fellowship status was unclear, the general otolaryngology script was used. Board certification was verified using the American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery certification tool (abohns.org/verify-certification); if the physician was not listed as certified, the caller asked whether the physician was board certified after an appointment was offered. Calls used the phone number listed on the practice website (to avoid inadvertently reaching a personal number listed in NPI/CMS/Academy records); when no website could be found, the caller used the NPI/CMS-listed number with the general script and noted the absence of a website. The practice city and 2020 RUCA code were recorded before the call (via the Rural Health Information Hub "Am I Rural?" tool), along with any additional practice cities and their RUCA codes.

**During the call.** The caller delivered the selected script (Table S9). If asked for identifying details, the caller gave a standardized identity, "John" or "Jessica Smith," date of birth June 1 of a script-appropriate year. **No appointment was ever booked:** when an appointment was offered, the caller requested the next-available date ("I want to make sure I can find an appointment that works with my schedule before moving forward with scheduling") to compute the business-day wait, then stated they would check their schedule and call back. Structured response handling captured whether the physician sees the presented complaint (and, if not, what they do see), whether another provider could be seen for the concern and whether that provider was a physician or advanced practice provider and the time to that appointment, whether the physician was not accepting new patients, redirection to a different provider, and whether the physician was no longer practicing (retired vs moved). *[Not specified in the script draft: the number and timing of call attempts before an office was recorded as unreachable, to confirm from the protocol.]*

**Table S9. Subspecialty-matched chief-complaint scripts (verbatim caller wording).**

| Subspecialty | Clinical scenario | Verbatim opening script |
|---|---|---|
| General otolaryngology | Nasal obstruction; suspected deviated septum after failed medical therapy | "I was worked up by my primary care doctor for difficulty breathing through my nose. I have tried multiple nasal sprays but none of them have helped. My primary care doctor said they think I have a deviated septum and referred me to Dr. ___." |
| Pediatric otolaryngology | 12-year-old with recurrent tonsillitis and snoring; tonsillectomy discussion | "My twelve-year-old son has been worked up for recurrent tonsillitis and snoring by our pediatrician. He has had seven episodes of tonsillitis in the last year. He is also now snoring loudly and seems very tired during the day. Our pediatrician referred us to Dr. ___ to discuss possible tonsillectomy." |
| Rhinology | Recurrent chronic sinusitis after prior sinus surgery; revision considered | "I have been evaluated and treated for chronic sinusitis by my primary care doctor and a general ENT. I have had one prior sinus surgery ten years ago, but my symptoms are back. I was referred to see Dr. ___ to discuss possible revision sinus surgery." |
| Otology/neurotology | 70-year-old parent with progressive hearing loss; cochlear-implant candidate | "My 70-year-old mother has been worked up for hearing loss by our audiologist and a general ENT. She has had progressive hearing loss and is no longer getting benefit from hearing aids. After her most recent hearing test, she was referred to Dr. ___ to discuss possible cochlear implantation." |
| Laryngology | 70-year-old parent with dysphonia; paralyzed vocal cord after cardiac surgery | "My 70-year-old father has been evaluated and treated for a hoarse voice by a general ENT and speech pathologist. He was told he has a paralyzed vocal cord after open heart surgery two years ago. He has completed a variety of treatments, but his voice has not improved. He is being referred to Dr. ___ to discuss possible surgical options for his voice." |
| Facial plastic surgery | Post-traumatic nasal deformity and obstruction; rhinoplasty evaluation | "I have been worked up for difficulty breathing through my nose and a change in the appearance of my nose after a car accident one year ago by my primary care doctor. I was referred to Dr. ___ to discuss possible surgical options to improve my breathing and shape of my nose." |
| Head and neck oncology | Thyroid nodule with biopsy showing high malignancy risk; thyroidectomy discussion | "I have been worked up for a thyroid nodule by my primary care provider. I had a biopsy done by an endocrinologist that showed a 70% chance of thyroid cancer. I was referred to Dr. ___ to discuss possible thyroidectomy." |
| Sleep medicine | No dedicated script | Because script selection followed fellowship training and no sleep-specific vignette existed, physicians classified as sleep medicine received the **general otolaryngology** script above. |
